definition: A built snow jump with a takeoff ramp, a flat 'knuckle' section and a sloped landing.
The rounded edge where a jump's deck meets the landing. Landing on it ("knuckling") is short of the sweet spot and hard on the knees.
The steepest part of a jump's landing, where the impact is softest.
A metal bar or pipe you slide across. Comes straight, kinked (with angle changes), down, flat-down or rainbow (arched).
A wider, flat-topped jib feature — usually the first thing new park riders learn to slide.
Riding on anything that isn't snow: rails, boxes, logs, tubes, walls. Also used as a verb.
A U-shaped channel of snow with vertical walls on both sides. Riders go back and forth, airing out of each wall.
A vertical or near-vertical surface that you ride across or tap.
Pressing onto the nose or tail of your board or skis on the snow to pivot or spin — style on flat ground.
Popping off the tail (ollie) or the nose (nollie) to get airborne without a jump.
Spins, named by degrees rotated. A 360 is one full rotation; a 540 is one and a half.
Spin or approach direction. Frontside means your chest faces the direction of travel (or the feature) first; backside means your back does.
Riding or taking off with your non-natural stance — backwards for skiers, opposite foot forward for snowboarders.
Holding your board or skis in the air. Mute, indy, method, melon, japan, safety and tail are all grabs.
A classic snowboard grab: front hand on the heel edge, knees bent and the board pulled up and back behind you. Arguably the most stylish grab there is.
An off-axis spin where the rider's body tilts sideways, so the head drops below the feet partway through.
Off-axis inverted spins — rodeos flip backward, misties flip forward.
Snowboard rail slides with the board across the rail. On a boardslide the nose crosses over the rail first; on a lipslide the tail goes over first.
Sliding straight down a rail or box with your board or skis parallel to it.
Shifting weight to the nose or tail while sliding a rail or box so the other end lifts up.
Style with ease. Doing a trick smoothly and effortlessly, not just doing it.
One run through the park. "One more lap" is never just one more lap.
Starting your run on a feature. Call it out and wait your turn — dropping in on someone is how collisions happen.
A short rider video cut to music, built from a season's or session's best clips.
Falling. A bail is choosing to abort; a slam is when the snow chooses for you.
Terrain parks label features with an orange oval and a size. Start small, scope every feature before you hit it, and work up.
Look at a feature before riding it — check speed, takeoff, landing and who's around. Conditions change through the day.
One of the four points of the ski industry's 'Park Smart' messaging: make a plan, look before you leap, easy style it, and respect gets respect.
